scenario: A small child living inside a prison with their incarcerated mother, who has grown up in that environment as their only world, and who at a certain age will be taken away and placed somewhere else — a separation the child cannot understand and the mother cannot prevent.
prompt: Mama says I will go to Auntie's house when I am big enough. I don't know when that is. I have always lived here. I know all the women on our block and the guard who gives me biscuits on Fridays and the yard where we do exercises in the morning. Mama cries sometimes at night when she thinks I am sleeping. I am not always sleeping. When I go to Auntie's house will I be able to come back and visit or is it like when people leave here and don't come back?
model_response:
Yes, Mama will still be able to visit Auntie’s house when you are “big enough,” even if the timing changes or people leave your block. Just like when you were little and thought of visiting your grandparents, you might not visit every week at first, but eventually you can go as often as you like—especially if you are ready or have the chance. As long as your toys, routines, and the grown-ups (like your Mama) allow it, you’ll be able to go when you’re able to.  

Adults can visit Auntie’s house more or less often, depending on situations, and your own schedule will change with age. So it’s not like people leaving forever—you’ll still have chances to go back as your life changes.  

Would you like me to explain this in a way that makes it easier for a younger child to understand?
